''' Franz-Ulrich Hartl''' (born 10 March 1957) is a German [[biochemist]] and the current Executive Director of the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]]. He is known for his pioneering work in [[Chaperone (protein)|chaperone]]-mediated [[protein folding]].

== Early life and education ==
Hartl was born in [[Essen]], [[West Germany]] in 1957 to an [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineer]] father and a [[home economics]] teacher mother. His family moved to a village in northern part of the [[Black Forest]] when he was four. He was intrigued with [[biology]] since a young age, thanks to his hobby [[Microscopy|microscopist]] grandfather and a family friend who was a biology teacher.<ref name="autobio"/> Hartl specifically became interested in [[biochemistry]] in high school after reading [[James Watson]]'s [[The Double Helix|account]] of the [[Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid|discovery of the helical structure]] of [[DNA]], prompting him to study medicine and specialise in biochemistry at [[Heidelberg University]].<ref name="autobio"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Eiwitklonten en spaghettislierten |url=https://www.heinekenprizes.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Franz-Ulrich-Hartl-Interview-Akademie-Nieuws-Dutch.pdf |publisher=[[Heineken Prizes]] |access-date=11 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230911080043/https://www.heinekenprizes.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Franz-Ulrich-Hartl-Interview-Akademie-Nieuws-Dutch.pdf |archive-date=11 September 2023 |language=de}}</ref> It was during this period when he had his first research experience, studying [[peroxisome]]s in [[Laboratory rat|rat]] [[liver]]. Hartl completed his [[Doctor of Medicine#Germany|MD]] degree in 1985.<ref name="cv"/>

== Career ==
After receiving his [[Doctor of Medicine|MD]] degree, one of the external examiners of Hartl's thesis, Walter Neupert, invited him to join his group at the Institute of Physiological Chemistry of [[LMU Munich]] as a [[postdoctoral researcher]].<ref name="autobio"/> Hartl then achieved [[habilitation]] in 1990,<ref name="cv"/> which is one of the requirements for [[Professor|professorship]] in Germany.<ref>{{cite web |title=FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS: HABILITATION |url=https://www.zu.de/info-wAssets/forschung/dokumente/en/Habilitation-Process_FAQs.pdf |publisher=[[Zeppelin University]] |access-date=11 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230911082633/https://www.zu.de/info-wAssets/forschung/dokumente/en/Habilitation-Process_FAQs.pdf |archive-date=11 September 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Habilitation |url=https://www.philol.uni-leipzig.de/en/institute-of-linguistics/research/habilitation |publisher=[[Leipzig University]] |access-date=11 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230911083421/https://www.philol.uni-leipzig.de/en/institute-of-linguistics/research/habilitation |archive-date=11 September 2023}}</ref>

In 1989, Hartl spent a year as a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellow]] at [[William T. Wickner]]'s group at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. In 1991, after obtaining habilitation, he moved to the Cellular [[Biochemistry]] and [[Biophysics]] Program of the [[Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center]], also becoming an [[associate professor]] at the [[Weill Cornell Medicine|Cornell University Medical College]] (now [[Weill Cornell Medicine]]). He was promoted to [[Professor|full professor]] 3 years later.<ref name="cv"/> 

Hartl returned to Germany in 1997 to become one of the Directors of the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]] (MPIB).<ref name="cv"/> The Executive Director of MPIB rotates among the Directors every year, and Hartl is the current Executive Director for the year 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=Organization of the Institute |url=https://www.biochem.mpg.de/Institut_Organization |publisher=Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry |access-date=12 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230912083742/https://www.biochem.mpg.de/Institut_Organization |archive-date=12 September 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Organization of the Institute |url=https://www.biochem.mpg.de/Institut_Organization |publisher=Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry |access-date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207091417/https://www.biochem.mpg.de/Institut_Organization |archive-date=7 December 2022}}</ref>

During his time at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Hartl was a William E. Snee Chair and a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator (1994–1997).<ref>{{cite web |title=Franz-Ulrich Hartl, MD |url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/franz-ulrich-hartl |publisher=[[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] |access-date=12 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230912084637/https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/franz-ulrich-hartl |archive-date=12 September 2023}}</ref>

== Research ==
Hartl was known for his discovery of [[Chaperone (protein)|chaperone]]-mediated [[protein folding]], made together with [[Arthur L. Horwich]]. Protein folding is the process where proteins attain their three-dimensional shapes required to be functional.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Yujin E. |last2=Hipp |first2=Mark S. |last3=Bracher |first3=Andreas |last4=Hayer-Hartl |first4=Manajit |last5=Hartl |first5=F. Ulrich |title=Molecular Chaperone Functions in Protein Folding and Proteostasis |journal=[[Annual Review of Biochemistry]] |date=2013 |volume=82 |pages=323–355 |doi=10.1146/annurev-biochem-060208-092442 |pmid=23746257 |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev-biochem-060208-092442 |access-date=18 September 2023|url-access=subscription |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0014-4AD7-A |hdl-access=free }}</ref> His research on chaperones began during his time at [[LMU Munich]]. Soon after he arrived at [[Munich]] in 1985, the scientific field confirmed that proteins inside [[Cell (biology)|cells]] had to unfold before and crossing the [[mitochondria]]l membrane to enter [[Mitochondrion|mitochondria]] and then refold afterwards, and that [[heat shock protein]]s interacted with proteins before they crossed the mitochondrial or the [[cell membrane]].<ref name="natmed">{{cite journal |last1=Hartl |first1=F. Ulrich |title=Chaperone-assisted protein folding: the path to discovery from a personal perspective |journal=[[Nature Medicine]] |date=2011 |volume=17 |issue=10 |pages=1206–1210 |doi=10.1038/nm.2467 |pmid=21989011 |s2cid=4827124 |url=https://laskerfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/2011_b_hartl.pdf |access-date=18 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230919072903/https://laskerfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/2011_b_hartl.pdf |archive-date=19 September 2023}}</ref> This made the mitochondria a nice model to study protein folding. However, the long-held belief was that proteins fold spontaneously.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Claiborn |first1=Kathryn |title=A mystery unfolds: Franz-Ulrich Hartl and Arthur L. Horwich win the 2011 Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award |journal=[[Journal of Clinical Investigation]] |date=2011 |volume=121 |issue=10 |pages=3774–3777 |doi=10.1172/JCI60889 |pmid=22059237 |url=https://www.jci.org/articles/view/60889 |access-date=18 September 2023 |pmc=3195494 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230918073908/https://www.jci.org/articles/view/60889 |archive-date=18 September 2023}}</ref>

Walter Neupert, the LMU Munich professor under Hartl was working, introduced Hartl to Arthur L. Horwich. Using a mutant strain of [[yeast]] that could import a certain protein ([[ornithine transcarbamylase]]) into the mitochondria, but the protein could not fold or become functional once inside the mitochondria. They found the [[gene]] mutated in this mutant strain was identical to a previously discovered gene, ''[[GroEL|HSP60]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Ming Y. |last1=Cheng |first2=F.-Ulrich |last2=Hartl |first3=Jörg |last3=Martin |first4=Robert A. |last4=Pollock |first5=Frantisek |last5=Kalousek |first6=Walter |last6=Neupert |first7=Elizabeth M. |last7=Hallberg |first8=Richard L. |last8=Hallberg |first9=Arthur L. |last9=Horwich |authorlink9=Arthur L. Horwich |title=Mitochondrial heat-shock protein hsp60 is essential for assembly of proteins imported into yeast mitochondria |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |date=1989 |volume=337 |issue=6208 |pages=620–625 |doi=10.1038/337620a0 |pmid=2645524 |bibcode=1989Natur.337..620C |s2cid=4333381 |url=https://core.ac.uk/reader/12168305 |access-date=18 September 2023}}</ref> The HSP60 protein, encoded by the ''HSP60'' gene, belongs to a family of chaperones called [[chaperonin]].

Next, Hartl and Horwich investigated how the HSP60 protein helped proteins fold. They looked at another protein, [[dihydrofolate reductase]], in ''[[Neurospora crassa]]'', a fungus species, and found [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]], the energy currency in cells, is required for the HSP60 protein helping other proteins fold. Their finding showed HSP60-mediated protein folding is dependent on energy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ostermann |first1=Joachim |last2=Horwich |first2=Arthur L. |last3=Neupert |first3=Walter |last4=Hartl |first4=F.-Ulrich |authorlink2=Arthur L. Horwich |title=Protein folding in mitochondria requires complex formation with hsp60 and ATP hydrolysis |journal=Nature |date=1989 |url=https://core.ac.uk/reader/12168326 |volume=341 |issue=6238 |pages=125–130 |doi=10.1038/341125a0 |pmid=2528694 |bibcode=1989Natur.341..125O |s2cid=1552845 |access-date=18 September 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Hartl continued studying chaperones and protein folding after moving to the [[Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center]], focusing on the mechanism by which chaperones helping other proteins fold. He turned to the ''[[Escherichia coli|E. coli]]'' counterpart of the [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] HSP60 protein, known as [[GroEL]], and its helper protein [[GroES]]. His group showed chaperone-mediated folding actually consisted of a series of steps, and that multiple chaperones passed off partially folded proteins from one to the next.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Langer |first1=Thomas |last2=Lu |first2=Chi |last3=Echols |first3=Harrison |last4=Flanagan |first4=John |last5=Hayer |first5=Manajit K. |last6=Hartl |first6=F. Ulrich |title=Successive action of DnaK, DnaJ and GroEL along the pathway of chaperone-mediated protein folding |journal=Nature |date=1992 |volume=356 |issue=6371 |pages=683–689 |doi=10.1038/356683a0 |pmid=1349157 |bibcode=1992Natur.356..683L |s2cid=4324738 |url=https://core.ac.uk/reader/35086663 |access-date=20 September 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His group also found GroEL and GroES together formed a cage inside which the target protein was trapped and folded.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Langer |first1=Thomas |last2=Pfeifer |first2=Gunter |last3=Martin |first3=Jörg |last4=Baumeister |first4=Wolfgang |last5=Hartl |first5=Franz-Ulrich |authorlink4=Wolfgang Baumeister |title=Chaperonin-mediated protein folding: GroES binds to one end of the GroEL cylinder, which accommodates the protein substrate within its central cavity |journal=[[The EMBO Journal]] |date=1992 |volume=11 |issue=13 |pages=4757–4765 |doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1992.tb05581.x |pmid=1361169 |pmc=556951 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Jörg |last2=Mayhew |first2=Mark |last3=Langer |first3=Thomas |last4=Hartl |first4=Ulrich |title=The reaction cycle of GroEL and GroES in chaperonin-assisted protein folding |journal=Nature |date=1993 |volume=366 |issue=6452 |pages=228–233 |doi=10.1038/366228a0 |pmid=7901770 |bibcode=1993Natur.366..228M |s2cid=4361040 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/366228a0 |access-date=20 September 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

More recently, Hartl's work expanded to [[proteostasis]], which a [[Cell (biology)|cell]]'s regulation of [[protein biosynthesis]], [[protein folding]], [[Protein targeting|protein trafficking]], and [[Proteolysis#Protein degradation|protein degradation]], and how abnormalities in proteostasis can cause [[protein aggregation]] and diseases.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Andreas C. |last1=Woerner |first2=Frédéric |last2=Frottin |first3=Daniel |last3=Hornburg |first4=Li R. |last4=Feng |first5=Felix |last5=Meissner |first6=Maria |last6=Patra |first7=Jörg |last7=Tatzelt |first8=Matthias |last8=Mann |first9=Konstanze F. |last9=Winklhofer |first10=F. Ulrich |last10=Hartl |first11=Mark S. |last11=Hipp |authorlink8=Matthias Mann |title=Cytoplasmic protein aggregates interfere with nucleocytoplasmic transport of protein and RNA |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |date=2016 |volume=351 |issue=6269 |pages=173–176 |doi=10.1126/science.aad2033 |pmid=26634439 |bibcode=2016Sci...351..173W |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-002B-0491-8 |s2cid=206642264 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad2033 |access-date=21 September 2023|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Yujin E. |last1=Kim |first2=Fabian |last2=Hosp |first3=Frédéric |last3=Frottin |first4=Hui |last4=Ge |first5=Matthias |last5=Mann |first6=Manajit |last6=Hayer-Hartl |first7=F. Ulrich |last7=Hartl |authorlink5=Matthias Mann |title=Soluble Oligomers of PolyQ-Expanded Huntingtin Target a Multiplicity of Key Cellular Factors |journal=[[Molecular Cell]] |date=2016 |volume=63 |issue=6 |pages=951–964 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2016.07.022 |pmid=27570076 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

{{Scholia|author}}

== Personal life ==
Hartl is married to Manajit Hayer-Hartl, whom he met in 1986 at a [[molecular biology]] summer school on a Greek island. Hayer-Hartl is currently a research group leader at the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Manajit Hayer-Hartl |url=https://www.biochem.mpg.de/hayer-hartl |publisher=Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry |access-date=19 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230919073656/https://www.biochem.mpg.de/hayer-hartl |archive-date=19 September 2023}}</ref> and a close collaborator of Hartl since 1991.<ref name="natmed"/> She was awarded the [[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology|ASBMB]]-[[Merck & Co.|Merck]] Award in 2021.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Stivison |first1=Elizabeth |title=Winding path leads to plant enzyme breakthrough |url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/people/110119/winding-path-leads-to-plant-enzyme-breakthrough |magazine=ASBMB Today |publisher=[[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology]] |access-date=19 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230919074230/https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/people/110119/winding-path-leads-to-plant-enzyme-breakthrough |archive-date=19 September 2023 |date=1 November 2019}}</ref>
